archetype.name: Playoff Team (possession-first)
archetype.definition: A club that drives play at 5-on-5 well enough to belong in the playoff field, even while its goal differential, power play and backup goaltending lag behind the process.

report.headline: The process finally matches the record; the power play and crease don't yet
report.take:
Montréal is 6-3-2 with a goal differential of exactly zero, and on its face that looks like a team living on overtime. Pts vs Goal Diff of 1.7, second in the league, says the standings are ahead of the scoreboard, and the results back it: a 1-0 overtime win over Detroit and two 4-3 overtime wins over Buffalo did a lot of the work. If that were the whole story, this would be a pretender card. It isn't the whole story.

The real change is underneath. The Canadiens are taking 54.1% of the 5-on-5 expected goals (9th) and 56% of the shot attempts (5th). Last season's 106-point team did it with a 47.9% xGF share and a 101.8 PDO, a team outrunning its play. This one is the reverse. Its all-situations PDO is 99.3 against a league mark of 100.6, the skaters are shooting 10.8% and the goalies are stopping 88.6% as a group. The percentages have been working against them. The overtime breaks have roughly offset that, which is why the differential sits at zero while the shot share points to a winning team.

Two things are holding the goal column down. The power play is converting 12.5%, 28th and well under the league's 21.2%, a strange collapse for a unit that ran at 23.1% last year. The other is the crease, which is really two stories. Jacob Fowler is fourth on the goalie tab with a .924 save % and 6.1 GSAx. Jakub Dobes sits at .847 and -6.2, so the starts split nearly evenly between an elite goalie and a sieve. The team-wide C+ in goal is an average of those two extremes.

The engine is the top of the lineup. Lane Hutson plays 25.53 minutes a night, is sixth among 250 defensemen and posts a 61% xGF share, and he carries an A- blueline. Nick Suzuki has 12 points in 9 games, and Cole Caufield has 6 goals on 36 shots. Depth forwards like Alex Newhook and Chris Kreider are getting caved in below 40% xGF, which keeps the forward grade at C+. The trajectory is good: the last five games produced a .700 points percentage and 2.8 goals allowed a game. With better luck on the power play and in net, the margin should start showing up on the scoreboard.

strengths.title: Driving play at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Montréal controls the puck and the chances, ranking 5th in CF % and 9th in xGF %. That is a sharp step up from last season's 47.9% xGF, when the results ran ahead of the play. With Hutson and Suzuki doing the heavy lifting, this is the most durable part of the profile, even over a small sample.

strengths.title: Hutson anchors an A- blueline
strengths.body: Lane Hutson is sixth among 250 defensemen on the site and plays more than 25 minutes a night with a 61% expected-goals share. Carrier and Guhle give the group real depth, which is why the blueline grades A- while the forwards sit at C+. It should last, though it leans heavily on one player's minutes.

strengths.title: Fowler is playing like a No. 1
strengths.body: Jacob Fowler has a .924 save %, a 1.79 GAA and 6.1 GSAx in six starts, fourth on the goalie tab. It's a short run, but it is the clearest single lever on this team's results. The more of the net he takes, the faster the differential catches up to the shot share.

concerns.title: A power play gone cold
concerns.body: The power play is converting 12.5%, 28th in the league and far below the 21.2% average. The unit ran at 23.1% last season, so this looks more like a slump than a ceiling. Still, it is the main reason a team that out-shoots opponents only has an even goal differential.

concerns.title: The Dobes starts are leaking goals
concerns.body: Jakub Dobes has a .847 save % and -6.2 GSAx in five starts, which cancels out everything Fowler has saved. That is why the team save % ranks 21st despite a top-five goalie on the roster. Unless Dobes steadies or the split tilts toward Fowler, this will keep costing games.

concerns.title: Standings ahead of the margin
concerns.body: The record carries 1.7 points more than the goal differential implies, second in the league, much of it from one-goal overtime wins. That kind of edge rarely holds. If the percentages don't turn, the standings could slide back toward a .500 goal differential.

trend.note: After the opening win came a three-game skid in which Montréal allowed five or six goals a night. The last five games went 3-1-1 at a .700 points percentage, with goals allowed down to 2.8 a game, capped by road wins in Chicago and Winnipeg.

weekAhead.headline: Two soft matchups bracket a trip into Dallas' wall
weekAhead.body:
The week opens on the road with St. Louis and Dallas, then returns home for Pittsburgh and Winnipeg. The Blues and Penguins are both middling clubs on the site (20th and 19th) with defenses that give up more than expected to forwards. Winnipeg was beaten 2-1 just this past weekend and is shooting only 8.4%, 30th.

Dallas is the problem. The Stars allow the fewest goals and shots in the league, save .928 as a team and hold forwards furthest under their expected points. A puck-possession team with a struggling power play can dominate attempts there and still lose 2-1. Taking care of the other three games is how this week turns positive.

keyMatchups.title: Suzuki against St. Louis' middle
keyMatchups.body: The Blues give up more to centers relative to expectation than all but one team, and centers take an outsized share of the points scored against them. Suzuki, with 12 points in 9 games, is set up to feast in the opener.

keyMatchups.title: Possession vs Dallas goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Dallas leads the league in save % and has 9.9 GSAx, and it allows only 21.5 shots a game. Montréal's shot share is real, but in this game it runs into a goalie group grading A+, and the 12.5% power play is unlikely to bail it out.

keyMatchups.title: Wingers vs Pittsburgh
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh ranks 29th in what it allows to wingers and beat Montréal 6-5 in overtime early in October. Caufield, Slafkovský and Bolduc should find room, though Montréal's own defense also gives up more than expected to wingers.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal on the back half of the trip. A Fowler-heavy week turns the possession edge into points; Dobes starts are where this team's goals against balloon.

restOfSeason.body:
The profile has flipped from last year's: the 5-on-5 play is now genuinely good, while the shooting, save and power-play percentages are below par. Some of that should correct. The power play has no history of being this bad, and Fowler gives the team a starter capable of lifting the save % well above the current team mark. Against that, the overtime luck in the standings will likely give some back. The pace of 104 points is reasonable, but it will be reached by a different route, with the goal differential turning positive while the close-game edge fades.

The ceiling depends on depth. A C+ forward group, with Newhook and Kreider underwater on expected goals, means the top line and Hutson carry too much. If the depth holds and Fowler takes the bulk of the starts, Montréal is a solid playoff team in a crowded Atlantic. If Dobes keeps splitting the net at .847, this is a bubble club with good shot metrics.
swingFactors: Power play recovering toward league average

confidence.note: Only 11 games, but the shot-share signal is strong and points one way.
